NextItNet uses causal dilated convolutions inside residual blocks, with normalization and activation placement varying by block design. Full-sequence receptive-field coverage cannot identify the dilation schedule: different schedules can reach every input while producing different values. Test exact layer outputs against an independent reference, rather than checking only dependency coverage. The [NextItNet paper](https://fajieyuan.github.io/papers/nextitnet6.pdf) describes both residual designs and left padding.

A proposed fault-specific oracle: implement convolution using explicit indexed sums, y[t,o] = b[o] + Σ W[o,c,j]x[t − p_left + jd,c], treating out-of-range indices as zero. Obtain expected dilation and padding from an independent specification, never the layer’s potentially mutated attributes. With kernel width k, causal length-preserving padding is p_left=(k−1)d, p_right=0. Probe each convolution before normalization with impulses at several positions, distinct nonzero tap weights, and multiple channels; compare amplitudes and offsets. Also compare random-input outputs. A dilation mutant that adjusts padding to preserve shape still changes these numerical results. Interior and boundary probes expose shifted asymmetric padding; future-input perturbations specifically expose noncausality.

For whole-block checks, reproduce the actual normalization/activation order and compare residual branch F(x), skip branch S(x), and their sum separately. Disable dropout; use multichannel, nonconstant inputs to avoid normalization or ReLU erasing signals. Compute normalization explicitly over channels at each batch/time position, checking epsilon and affine parameters; perturb other times and batch members to expose unintended normalization axes. Apply the architecture’s padding masks at their specified locations, including after biased operations where required. Check left-padded histories and final-nonpadding readout. These are proposed tests derived from the architecture, not reported mutation-testing results.
